title: The Roads
text: The question this section was meant to answer is where pumas are killed by vehicles. That question cannot be answered here yet, because the data that would answer it are not in hand. So this section does two things instead: it states what is missing, and it presents the best interim proxy — where the corridor and dangerous roads coincide.

title: The Roads
text:
What is missing?
Direct roadkill records for the Bay Area are held in the California Roadkill Observation System (CROS), maintained by the UC Davis Road Ecology Center. A data request has been made with data pending. The project does not scrape or reconstruct those records — they are used with authorisation. Until the data has been shared, there is no published mortality-point layer in this project. When the CROS records are available, they will overlay the risk surface below as a validation layer — confirming or correcting where the proxy points.

title: The Roads
section: The interim proxy — where traffic meets the corridor
text:
The interim proxy — where traffic meets the corridor
What the analysis can say comes from combining two things: how busy each road is (traffic volume, from the crossing analysis in the connectivity section) and whether that road sits inside the core corridor, where a puma is most likely to actually move. Collision risk is highest where both are true.
The connectivity section ranked road crossings by traffic, and several busy roads appeared near the top. But most of those busy roads clip the corridor at its permeable edges, not through its core. When the core-corridor filter is applied, the risk narrows sharply.








Figure 1: Collision-risk proxy: road crossings where traffic and the core corridor coincide. Crossings inside the core corridor are coloured by traffic volume (blue for quiet to magenta for busy); crossings outside the core are greyed — they are barriers, but not where a puma is most likely to cross. US-101 at Coyote Valley is the one crossing that is both high-traffic and inside the core corridor, which makes it the clear top collision risk.




The map makes the filter visible. Most of the busy roads the corridor crosses are grey, because they clip the corridor outside its core. What is coloured — busy and in the core — is dominated by one road: US-101 at Coyote Valley. It is the single crossing that is both high-traffic and inside the core corridor, and so it is the clear top collision-risk location, not merely the top barrier.

title: The Roads
text:
The risk ranking
Ranking the crossings by the two factors together — traffic volume and core-corridor membership — puts US-101 alone at the top. The next-busiest roads fall away because they sit outside the core; the other in-core roads are quiet.

Top road crossings by traffic and core-corridor overlap. Only US-101 is both high-traffic and in-core — the combination that defines collision risk. Traffic values are directly measured; see the connectivity section for the full confidence-tiered ranking.

title: Movement
text:
The puma (Puma concolor), also called mountain lion, cougar, or panther, is the large cat of the Bay Area. An adult male can weigh 60 kilograms and needs a very large home range — often more than 100 square kilometres. Pumas are solitary and hunt mostly deer. They avoid people and rarely stay near development. That large space requirement is the whole problem this section studies: a puma must cross roads and developed ground to move between habitat blocks, and the Bay Area is cut through with both. Where the landscape still lets an animal pass is the connectivity question.
The puma question is the opposite of the bobcat one. There are too few puma records to model where the animals are, and the precise locations that do exist are sensitive enough that publishing them would do harm. So this section does not map where pumas were seen. It maps where the landscape would let one move.

title: Movement
text:
Built from resistance
Every layer in this section rests on a resistance surface: a map of how costly each 1 km cell is for a puma to cross, high where the land is developed, steep, or busy with roads, low where it is protected open ground. The surface is assembled from land cover, terrain, human modification, and traffic.
The bobcat occupancy model had to correct for recording effort, because it was built from sightings. The puma corridors carry no effort term at all — there are no sightings in them to be biased. Where the puma corridors agree with a density surface, they agree for a structural reason. This is explained more while answering Question 5.

title: Movement
section: Why you see a band, not a line?
text:
Why you see a band, not a line?
The core result is a corridor between the two largest habitat blocks in the region: the Santa Cruz Mountains and the southern Diablo Range, linked across the south Bay through the Coyote Valley pinch where US-101 cuts the gap. The least-cost path between them runs 37.2 km and passes within 1.6 km of the verified Coyote Valley crossing.
But the maps below show a band, not that line. A least-cost path is a single-cell-wide thread through a 1 km grid. It looks precise, and that precision is false: move the input weights a little and the line shifts by a kilometre or more. The actual result is the swath — the zone of low-cost cells around the path — shown in two tiers:

a core band (the lowest-cost 2% of corridor cells, 409 km²) — high-confidence corridor,
a context band (the lowest-cost 5%, 1,021 km²) — the permeable flanks around it.

The swath shows that the corridor runs through here, in this zone, not the corridor is this exact line. The precise pinch at Coyote Valley is located separately, by road geometry in the crossing analysis below.








Figure 1: The Santa Cruz Mountains ↔︎ southern Diablo Range puma corridor, shown as a two-tier swath over the protected core habitat it connects. The darker core band is the lowest-cost 2% of corridor cells (409 km²), a high-confidence corridor; the lighter context band is the lowest-cost 5% (1,021 km²), the permeable flanks around it. Faint green blocks are the 164 core habitat patches; the two bold-outlined blocks are the corridor endpoints — Santa Cruz Mountains and the southern Diablo Range. The corridor runs through this zone. The precise US-101 pinch at Coyote Valley is located by road geometry in the crossing map below.

title: Movement
section: Where does the corridor meet the roads?
text:
Where does the corridor meet the roads?
A corridor is only as good as its worst crossing. Where the swath meets a major road, the road is a barrier whose severity scales with traffic. So each crossing is ranked by traffic volume.
The top barrier is US-101 at Coyote Valley, at 142,000 vehicles a day. Getting that number right took a correction. An earlier version of the analysis, using a spatial traffic-data join, dropped US-101 here to a modelled floor of about 80,000 — a 43% underestimate — and let a lower-traffic arterial outrank it. The fix referenced the traffic data along the highway route by postmile, recovered the real 142k, and re-ran the corridor analysis. US-101 is now correctly the top-ranked crossing.
Crossings are ranked within traffic-data confidence tiers, not on the raw number alone. A road whose volume is measured directly outranks one whose volume is filled in by name-matching, even when the filled-in number is close. This stops a lower-confidence estimate from masquerading as the top barrier.








Figure 2: Where the puma corridor crosses roads, ranked by traffic, zoomed to the crossing zone in the south Bay. All 290 crossing segments are shown where line thickness scales with traffic volume (AADT) and solid lines are directly-measured volumes while dashed lines are estimated (modeled, name-filled, or spatially filled — lower-confidence). The four named roads the corridor crosses are outlined and labelled; US-101 at Coyote Valley, at 142,000 vehicles a day, is the top barrier by a wide margin.

title: Movement
text:
The network
Widening from the single corridor to the whole system of large habitat blocks — the 29 cores of at least 30 km² — gives a connectivity network: each core linked to its geometric neighbours, each link routed through the resistance surface. Two findings come out of it.
Coyote Valley is the efficient link, and the traffic barrier — but not the structural weak point. The cheapest connections in the network — the strongest links — run through the south Bay, between the cores on either side of the Coyote Valley gap. That is where the two halves of the region connect at low cost. Those south-Bay links are the efficient path; the cross-bay alternatives cost far more. So Coyote Valley matters twice — as the real, protectable connection, and as the 142k traffic barrier astride it — but it is a strong link, not a weak one.
The structural weak links are the cross-bay spans. The costliest connections in the network are the long, high-resistance routes that would join the Peninsula / Santa Cruz cluster to the East-Bay / Diablo cluster across the central urbanized Bay — spans of 40 to 60 km with no stepping stones between them. The central Bay effectively splits the system into two subnetworks, joined efficiently only at the south end, through Coyote Valley. This matches what is already known: Santa Cruz Mountains pumas are famously isolated, connected to the Diablo Range mainly via the south Bay.
To summarize, Coyote Valley is a traffic-mitigation priority — a real corridor with a dangerous road across it. The cross-bay gaps are a fragmentation finding — evidence of what is already disconnected.
And the cross-bay links are not corridors to build. A 60 km least-cost path across the developed bayshore is at the edge of biological plausibility. The network method forces a route between geometric neighbours whether or not a real one exists, and the routing dutifully finds the least-bad line across an essentially impassable barrier. Those longest cross-bay links mean these clusters are effectively disconnected. The south-Bay connection, by contrast, is a real connection worth protecting.








Figure 3: The puma core-connectivity network over the core habitat it links. Faint green blocks are the core habitat patches. Links between cores are drawn as schematic lines coloured by cost — green links are cheap and strong (the efficient south-Bay connections), red links are costly and weak. The lines show connectivity topology, not exact routes: at a 1 km grain a single-cell path would imply false precision, so the lines say which cores connect and how cheaply. The three-to-five costliest links — the structural weak points — are shown instead as red swaths. The red cross-bay swaths are evidence of disconnection, not as corridors to protect.

title: Movement
text:
Limitations
These corridors are hypotheses about movement drawn from a landscape-cost model, not tracks from collared animals. Shifting the model’s weights within a plausible range moves the corridor by up to about 1.5 km, so the routes are stable in location but not exact to the metre. They are the best structural estimate of where connectivity runs — a well-founded hypothesis, and the right basis for asking where to look and where to protect.
Every puma layer here is shown as generalised geometry — bands and routes. That is deliberate and required: precise puma locations are a poaching and disturbance risk, so the project never publishes them. Nothing in this section is fine enough to reverse-engineer a den, a kill site, or a camera. The corridors are about where an animal could move, at the scale of the landscape, not about where any individual animal is.

title: Data & references
text:
Every map on this site is built from public, open-source data. This page describes what those datasets are, where they come from, and how they are licensed, and then lists the literature the analysis and narrative rest on. The full version — version strings, file paths, record counts, access dates, and known issues — is in docs/data-sources.md.
Two principles govern the data on this project. First, Phase 1 uses open data only — no partner or restricted data is used or published. Second, no precise puma location is ever published (see the note at the foot of this page).
All associated files — code, analysis scripts, documentation, and data-acquisition steps — are in the project repository at github.com/K-bsub/bay-area-wildcats.

title: Data & references
text:
The data

Where animals were recorded

GBIF (Global Biodiversity Information Facility) — the main occurrence source, pulled as a citable, DOI-stamped download, so the exact record set is reproducible. Records carry a coordinate-uncertainty value that the analysis respects when snapping points to units.
iNaturalist — community wildlife observations. iNaturalist obscures many sensitive species by default, but not mountain lions in California, which is exactly why the sensitive-data handling on this project is strict.
GBIF target-group background — for the bobcat occupancy model, a second, much larger GBIF pull of all vertebrate records across the region stands in for “where did people look at all,” which is what lets the model separate effort from presence.



Where habitat is protected

CPAD (California Protected Areas Database) — parks, preserves, watershed lands and other fee-owned open space, with the unit hierarchy the occupancy site definition needs.
CCED (California Conservation Easement Database) — conservation easements on otherwise private land, held as a separate layer and combined with CPAD for total protected coverage.
TIGER/Line county boundaries (US Census, via tigris) — the ten-county study frame.



What the landscape is made of?

ESA WorldCover 2021 — 10 m land cover (trees, shrub, built-up, cropland, and so on), the base habitat layer. A known trade-off: WorldCover under-maps California chaparral badly compared with older US products, which is why urban-intensity comes from human modification instead.
Global Human Modification (gHM) v3, 2022 (Theobald et al. 2024) — a 0–1 index of how heavily each area is modified by people; the dominant term in the puma resistance surface.
SILVIS housing density — block-level housing as a second human-footprint source.
AWS Terrain Tiles (via elevatr) — elevation, from which slope is derived. The tiles blend several public elevation sources at roughly 30 m effective resolution here.



Roads and traffic

OpenStreetMap roads (Geofabrik NorCal extract) — the road network, classified by type. Because roads are a barrier only when busy, road presence alone is not enough.
Caltrans AADT — annual average daily traffic counts, which turn “a road is here” into “how much traffic crosses here.” A structural caveat: traffic count stations cluster on busy roads, so any spatial fill of the gaps has a built-in upward bias, handled with a source flag.



Road mortality (pending)

CROS (California Roadkill Observation System) / UC Davis Road Ecology Center — the intended wildlife–vehicle collision source. Record-level access is still pending, so the collision-risk question is currently answered as a risk-overlap proxy, not as a mortality point layer.



Population context
There is no repeated regional census of Bay Area pumas or bobcats — nothing like the national tiger census that anchors the sister project. A single statewide puma abundance estimate exists (the California Mountain Lion Project, roughly 3,200–4,500 statewide) and is cited only as one-time context. No statewide bobcat abundance estimate exists at all.

title: Data & references
text:
Sensitive data






ImportantNo precise puma locations are published



iNaturalist does not obscure mountain lions in California, so this project holds precise puma records that could expose real animals if published as points. Published puma outputs are therefore always generalised — continuous surfaces at a 1 km grain, or summaries at the open-space-unit level — never point maps, camera locations, den sites, or kill sites. Bobcat data, lower-sensitivity, is published at finer resolution but reviewed under the same process. The full policy is in docs/sensitive-data-policy.md.


The complete data provenance, including every version, access date, DOI, and known issues, is in docs/data-sources.md; the full literature bibliography is in docs/references.md.

title: The Protected-Land
text: How much protected open space is there in the ten-county Bay Area, how is it held, and how does it break apart when you look at it the way a wide-ranging carnivore would — as a set of patches large enough to hold a home range, or not?

title: The Protected-Land
text:
Two kinds of protection
Protected land here comes in two forms, and the difference matters for a puma. Fee land is owned outright for conservation: the parks, watershed lands, and open-space preserves that most people picture. Easement land is private ground — often working ranchland — where the owner has sold or donated the right to develop it, so it stays open. To a puma crossing it, an easement grazing parcel next to a fee preserve is one continuous piece of habitat. Tenure is a legal distinction, not an ecological one.
The project keeps both. The connectivity track uses a union of the two sources: CPAD fee land and CCED conservation easements, merged into one protected-land layer, with fee taking precedence wherever the two map the same ground so no area is counted twice.

title: The Protected-Land
section: How much, and how much is new
text:
How much, and how much is new
The union holds 5,996.5 km² of protected land across the ten counties. Fee land accounts for 4,720.8 km² of that, spread over 1,129 CPAD units. The easements add 1,275.7 km² of genuinely new protected ground — a roughly 27% increase over the fee footprint alone — after removing 498.2 km² where easements overlapped land already protected in fee.
Conservation easements are not a rounding error on the map of Bay Area protected land. More than a quarter of the connectivity land — much of it working ranchland along the inner Coast Ranges — exists only because of easements. Leave them out and the protected-land picture looks substantially more fragmented than it is.
One limit on this comes with the easement data. Where the easement layer has no record, that does not mean the land is unprotected — only that no easement is mapped there. The union labels tenure where the data exists; it does not fill gaps. Read the easement totals as a floor, not a full accounting.

title: The Protected-Land
section: From protected land to habitat patches
text:
From protected land to habitat patches
A wide-ranging carnivore does not experience protected land as a legal inventory. It experiences it as patches — connected pieces of open ground it can settle in or move through. So the next step dissolves the union: fee and easement melt together wherever they touch, and the result is cut into distinct patches by physical contiguity, not by ownership.
Most of those patches are small. The patch-area distribution is a smooth size continuum, from thousands of tiny fragments up to a handful of very large blocks, with no natural break to filter on. A break would let the data choose the threshold; there isn’t one, so the threshold comes from the animal instead.
A puma home range spans tens to hundreds of square kilometres. A protected patch smaller than about 5 km² cannot hold a meaningful fraction of even one such range, so it works as a stepping-stone at most, not as a place a resident animal lives. Setting that 5 km² floor leaves 164 core patches large enough to anchor a home range. The floor still retains 82.5% of all protected area, because the area that gets dropped sits in thousands of tiny fragments that together hold very little ground.
The map below shows the whole dataset in three layers: the fee-owned CPAD land and the CCED easements underneath (each toggleable), and the 164 core patches drawn prominently on top. Hover any core patch for its name and area. Toggle the two tenure layers to see how much of the connectivity land — much of it inner-Coast-Range ranchland — exists only because of easements.








Figure 1: The ten-county protected-land dataset in three layers. Fee-owned CPAD land (green) and CCED conservation easements (gold) form the protected base; toggle each with the control at top-right. The 164 core patches — protected blocks of at least 5 km², large enough to anchor a puma home range — are drawn in dark outline on top; hover any one for its name and area. The two named corridor endpoints (Santa Cruz Mountains, southern Diablo Range) are called out.




Turn the easement layer off and the map opens up with gaps along the inner Coast Ranges — that missing ground is the 27% of the fabric that easements carry. Turn it back on and those gaps close. The two named cores, the Santa Cruz Mountains and the southern Diablo Range, are the endpoints the puma connectivity section links.








Figure 2: Patch count against the minimum-area floor. Each candidate floor is plotted with the number of patches that survive it; the amber point marks the chosen 5 km² floor, which keeps 164 patches and 82.5% of all protected area. The curve is a smooth continuum with no natural break, so the floor is set by the puma home-range scale rather than by a gap in the data.





This plot shows how many patches survive each candidate threshold, and the 5 km² cut is not severe. Most of what the floor removes is thousands of tiny fragments; the protected area they hold barely moves the total.
This is the structural shape of the problem. Of nearly 4,000 protected patches, only 164 are large enough to anchor a wide-ranging carnivore, and the habitat value concentrates in a small number of very large cores — the Santa Cruz Mountains block at 177 km², the southern Diablo Range at 500 km², and a short list of others. The rest of the protected fabric is stepping-stones and fragments between them.

title: The Protected-Land
section: What this section does not describe?
text:
What this section does not describe?
This is a description of the protected land, built from protected-area boundaries alone. What it does not tell you is whether an animal can actually move between those 164 cores. A patch being large is not the same as a patch being reachable. Two cores can sit a few kilometres apart on the map and be effectively cut off from each other by a freeway, a reservoir, or the developed bayshore.

title: Limitations
text: This page collects the limits that apply to the maps on this site. The limitations fall into two kinds: what the corridor can and cannot show, and what the descriptive maps (density, hot spots) can and cannot indicate. A short note on the data inputs follows.

title: Limitations
text:
The corridor is a hypothesis

No animal was tracked. The corridor is built entirely from the landscape — land cover, human modification, slope, and traffic. This project has no GPS-collar or telemetry data of its own. So the corridor is a modelled hypothesis about where movement is cheapest. Strong validation would need collar data showing animals using the route.
The route is weighted by author-set priors. The resistance surface blends its inputs on weights chosen by the analyst (45% human modification, 40% land cover, 15% slope), with directions and the traffic transform taken from published Santa Cruz Mountains puma work. The weights are sourced and reasonable, but they are priors, not fitted values — this project has no local movement data to fit them against.


How much the route can move: about 1.5 km
The corridor’s location is stable; its exact centre-line is not. When the gHM/land-cover weight was perturbed by ±10%, the broad corridor barely changed — the worst-case overlap of the wide context band stayed very high (IoU 0.941). But the single least-cost line shifted, and under gHM-heavy weighting, the path shortened from 37.2 km to 35.6 km, about 1.5 km.


The core-connectivity network has a cross-bay artifact
A second connectivity product — the network graph linking large habitat cores — carries a specific, named artifact.

The network is built with a Gabriel graph, which connects cores that are geometric neighbours. Across the central Bay, that forces edges over the water, which is an impassable barrier for a puma. So the longest cross-bay links in the network are not candidate corridors — but that those clusters are disconnected.
The ranking of links by cost is valid within the graph, the two-subnetwork finding (the central Bay splits a Peninsula / Santa Cruz Mountains subnetwork from an East Bay / Diablo one, joined efficiently only at the south) matches known Santa Cruz Mountains puma isolation.

title: Limitations
section: The descriptive maps are shaped by where people looked
text:
The descriptive maps are shaped by where people looked
The density (KDE) and hot-spot (Gi*) maps describe records, and records are made by people, unevenly. This is the effort problem, and it is the subject of its own page.

Every descriptive surface is effort-shaped. A warm density zone or a red hot spot can mean “many animals” or “many observers.” The two analyses handle this differently — the bobcat occupancy model removes the effort signal, so it diverges from the raw density; the puma corridor never contains an effort layer, so its convergence with the raw density is informative.
The puma hot-spot map is about half effort. Of the puma record hot-spots, only a minority survive the effort cross-check as trusted.
The convergence is corroboration, not proof. Where the corridor and the record density agree, part of that agreement is structural — both rest on the same land-cover and human-modification gradient.

title: Limitations
text:
Data-input limits
These are smaller, but each shapes a specific result.

Chaparral is under-mapped — but it does not move the corridor. The land-cover source (ESA WorldCover) badly under-maps California chaparral, prime cat habitat. This sounds serious for a habitat model. A pre-registered sensitivity test bounded it: rebuilding the resistance surface with chaparral treated as good habitat changed the corridor essentially not at all (overlap IoU 1.000 / 0.998). So the under-mapping is immaterial to connectivity.
Traffic counts are biased upward off the highways. Measured traffic covers state highways; local and arterial roads are filled in from the nearest measured segment or a class-based floor (about 19,851 segments spatially filled, and roughly 45% on a modelled floor). Because count stations cluster on busy roads, that fill runs high. The effect is compressed by the log-inverse traffic transform and bounded by a sensitivity check, but it is a real property of the data, tracked with a source flag on every segment.

title: Limitations
text:
Two questions left open

Road mortality is incomplete. The wildlife–vehicle collision question is currently answered as a risk-overlap proxy, because record-level roadkill data is still pending.
No population trend is possible. There is no repeated regional census of either species. A one-time statewide puma estimate exists as context; no statewide bobcat estimate exists at all.


Every limitation above is recorded in full, with its sensitivity test and its figures, in docs/methodology.md.

title: Methods
text:
This page explains the four main methods behind the maps on this site. The full processing log, every parameter value, and the numbered decisions are in docs/methodology.md.
One idea runs through all four: a record is not the animal. Every method here starts from points that people reported — where a puma or a bobcat was seen or photographed. People do not look everywhere equally. So each method is, in part, a way to deal with that unevenness. Two of the methods below describe the records; one tries to remove the effort from them; one does not use the records at all.

title: Methods
text:
Kernel density Estimation (KDE)
What it is. Kernel density turns a scatter of points into a smooth surface. At every place on the map it asks: how many records are near here, and how near? Close records count for more than far ones. The result is a heat surface — warm where records cluster, cool where they are sparse.






Figure 1: A worked kernel-density surface. The green circles are the raw point records. The grey bands are the density surface built from them — darker where points are dense, fading outward. Two dense cores are joined by a lower-density bridge, with a small outlying blob below. The bandwidth sets how far each point’s influence spreads, and so how much the cores merge or stay separate.



Illustration from Spatial Analysis Online (de Smith, Goodchild & Longley).
The one setting that matters: bandwidth. Bandwidth is the width of the smoothing. A narrow bandwidth hugs each point tightly and gives a spiky surface; a wide bandwidth blurs the points together into broad zones. The choice changes the map, so it must be made on a rule, not by eye.






TipWorked example — the two cats used different bandwidths



For bobcat, an automatic selector (bw.ppl) passed the pre-set rule and chose a bandwidth of about 1,110 m. Bobcat records are dense, so a tight smoothing still gives a stable surface.
For puma, the same automatic selectors failed the rule — they returned values so small (as low as 49 m) that the surface would have been a scatter of pinpricks, not a density. So the bandwidth was set from biology instead: about 5,000 m. This is why the puma density map shows broad warm regions, not sharp spots.


What it can and cannot tell you. KDE shows where records concentrate. It does not show where animals are, because the records are effort-shaped — warm can mean “many pumas” or “many observers.” On this site the KDE surfaces are always read with that caveat, and the puma KDE is used only as a cross-check, never as a distribution result.

title: Methods
text:
Hot spots (Getis-Ord Gi*)
What it is. A hot-spot statistic asks a sharper question than KDE: is the clustering here more than you would expect by chance? For each open-space unit, Gi* compares that unit and its neighbours against the whole study area. A unit with a high count, surrounded by other high-count units, becomes a statistically significant hot spot. The reverse — low counts among low counts — is a cold spot.
“Neighbours” has to be defined. A unit’s Gi* score depends on which units count as its neighbours. Here, neighbours are units within a set distance (about 6,342 m), with a floor so that even a remote unit still has some neighbours to compare against.
Why the correction matters. Testing over a thousand units at once means some will look “significant” by pure luck. A false-discovery-rate correction (Benjamini-Hochberg) tightens the bar so the surviving hot spots are ones you can trust are real clustering, not chance.






Figure 2: The Getis-Ord Gi* flow, panel by panel. Input data — a value per unit (here median income, a generic example). Z-scores — each unit scored on how far its neighbourhood sum sits from the study-area average; strong positive (brown) and strong negative (purple) stand out. P-values — how likely each score is by chance. Hot spots — the final map, keeping only units that pass the significance bar: red are hot (high-value clusters), blue are cold (low-value clusters), pale is not significant.



Illustration from the UCGIS GIS&T Body of Knowledge (Hot Spots and Getis-Ord Gi* Analysis). The example maps income, not wildlife — the method is the same.






TipWorked example — the effort check on top



A record hot spot has two possible causes: real animals, or hard surveying. So each hot spot is cross-read against a map of survey effort. If a unit is a record hot spot and an effort hot spot, it is flagged suspect — it may just be where people looked. If it is a record hot spot but not an effort hot spot, it is trusted. On the Effort page you can see this split drawn directly: solid units are trusted, dashed units are suspect.


What it can and cannot tell you. Gi* tells you where clustering is stronger than chance, and — with the effort check — how much of that is likely real. It still rests on the same effort-shaped records, so the effort flag is part of the result.

title: Methods
text:
Occupancy modelling
What it is. Occupancy modelling is the one method here that tries to remove the effort problem instead of just flagging it. It splits the question into two parts and fits them in order:

Detection. Given that a bobcat is present in a unit, how likely was it to be recorded, given how much people surveyed there? This is fitted first, with presence held constant, so the model learns the shape of the effort curve.
Occupancy. With the detection part fixed, the model then estimates the probability the animal is actually present, corrected for that effort.

The output is a presence surface that has the survey effort taken out — which is why it can, and does, disagree with the raw record density.
The two parts are two linked equations. For a unit \(i\) and a visit \(j\):
\[
\underbrace{z_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\psi_i)}_{\text{occupancy: is the unit occupied?}}
\qquad
\underbrace{y_{ij} \mid z_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(z_i \, p_{ij})}_{\text{detection: was the animal recorded, if present?}}
\]

\(\psi_i\) is the probability the unit is occupied — what we want.
\(p_{ij}\) is the probability of recording the animal on a visit, given it is present. This is where survey effort enters.
\(z_i\) is the true (hidden) presence, 0 or 1. The term \(z_i\,p_{ij}\) encodes the key rule: you can only detect what is there — if \(z_i = 0\), no record is possible, and a non-record where \(z_i = 1\) is a missed detection, not an absence.

Each side is modelled on covariates through a logit link — occupancy on habitat (\(\text{logit}(\psi_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i}\)) and detection on effort (\(\text{logit}(p_{ij}) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \, \text{effort}_{ij}\)). Fitting the detection side first is what lets the model tell “the animal was absent” apart from “nobody looked.”






TipWorked example — bobcat



The bobcat detection part was fitted first. A term for recording effort (the number of prior records in a unit) beat a no-effort model by a wide margin (about 408 AICc units — a very strong preference), confirming effort really does shape the raw records. With that fixed, the presence model was fitted over 845 open-space units. The result is the ψ (psi) surface on the Bobcat page — and it barely correlates with the raw density map (r = 0.075), because the model pulled the effort curve out.


Why puma does not get this. Occupancy modelling needs enough repeat records per unit to separate detection from presence. Puma records are too few and too obscured for a defensible fit, so the puma track uses connectivity (below) instead.
What it can and cannot tell you. Occupancy gives the cleanest presence estimate on the site, but only for bobcat, and only where enough units had repeat surveys — 284 units could not be modelled and are drawn as a distinct grey, never as “low occupancy.”

title: Methods
text:
Cost-corridor (puma connectivity)
What it is. The puma corridor is built from the landscape, not from records. It answers a movement question: if a puma travels between two large habitat cores, which route costs it the least? “Cost” here means difficulty of movement — open built-up land and busy roads are expensive to cross; forest and shrub are cheap.
It is a three-step process, and the map below shows all three.

Resistance surface (the input). Every 1 km cell is scored 1–100 for how hard it is to move through. The score is a weighted blend: 45% human modification, 40% land cover, 15% slope, with busy roads overriding the blend where they cross. 1 is freely permeable (good forest); 100 is a wall (dense city, a major freeway).
Cost-corridor surface (the output). From the resistance surface, the model accumulates the total cost of routing between the two cores, in both directions. Low values trace the preferential route; high values are off-route.






NoteWhat ‘least-cost’ actually means



Think of the resistance surface as terrain where every 1 km step has a price — cheap through forest, costly across a freeway. The least-cost path is the route between the two cores whose total price is lowest, the same idea as a sat-nav finding the shortest drive, except the “distance” is movement difficulty, not kilometres.
The algorithm works outward from a core, giving every cell its cumulative cost — the cheapest running total to reach it from the core. Do this from both cores and add the two surfaces, and each cell then holds the cost of the best route through it from core to core. That summed surface is the cost-corridor. The single cheapest line through it is the least-cost path; the low-cost slice around that line is the swath. A swath is used, because the exact line is a fragile artifact — shift one weight slightly and it hops a cell — while the slice is stable.


The swath (the published product). The swath is simply the lowest-cost slice of the cost-corridor surface — the cheapest ~5% of cells to move through (a narrower core ~2% inside it). That slice, drawn as a band, is the corridor you see on the Puma page.







NoteWhy the corridor uses no records



Because resistance is built only from land cover, human modification, slope, and traffic, the corridor never “sees” where pumas were reported. That is deliberate: it means when the corridor lands on the observed record density (the Effort page convergence finding), the agreement was not built in.


The map below shows the chain. The resistance surface (the input) underneath, the cheapest-route cost-corridor over it, and the two-tier swath outline on top.








Figure 3: The puma connectivity method, in three layers. Base: the movement-resistance surface (1 = freely permeable, 100 = near-impassable), built from human modification, land cover, slope, and major roads. Middle: the cost-corridor surface, the accumulated least-cost of routing between the two habitat cores. Top: the two-tier swath outline — the lowest-cost slice of that surface (core ≤ q2%, context ≤ q5%), which is the corridor published on the Puma page.




You can toggle the three layers with the control at top-right — turn the resistance base off to see the cheapest-route cost-corridor alone, or turn everything off but the swath to see the published corridor. The point of stacking them is to make the chain legible: the corridor is not drawn by hand, and it is not drawn from sightings; it falls out of the landscape, one step at a time.

title: Methods
text:
Where the detail lives
Every choice on this page — the bandwidth rule, the neighbour distance, the model sets, the resistance weights and their sources, and the sensitivity checks that tested them — is recorded as a numbered decision in docs/methodology.md, with the data sources in docs/data-sources.md and the layer schemas in docs/data-dictionary.md.

title: Wild Cats at the Urban Edge
text:
Pumas and bobcats have lived in California for thousands of years. Both were hunted heavily after European settlement. California paid a bounty on pumas from 1907 to 1963, and more than 12,000 animals were killed under it. Bobcats were trapped for their fur. The state changed course in the 1960s and 1970s: the puma bounty ended in 1963, sport hunting of pumas stopped in 1972, and a 1990 ballot measure made the puma a specially protected species. Bobcat trapping for fur continued longer; California banned commercial bobcat trapping in 2015 and banned bobcat hunting in 2020. Today neither species is recovering from near-extinction. The conservation question in the Bay Area is different — not how to bring them back, but how they keep moving and coexisting at the edge of a large city.
The two wild cats share the same ecosystem in the San Francisco Bay Area, and they present opposite analysis challenges. Bobcats are common and occurrence data are plenty. Pumas are rare, wide-ranging, and their precise locations are a risk to publish. One landscape has two data situations that point in different directions. This project analyses them separately.

title: Wild Cats at the Urban Edge
text:
What is studied?
Identifying Conservation Success Stories studied tiger recovery in select reserves in India. That study had a national census: five repeated survey rounds that made “population change over time” the question to ask.
The Bay Area has no equivalent for either species. There is one recent statewide mountain lion abundance estimate and no statewide bobcat estimate at all.
What the region does have is dense, well-kept open-source data on land protection, road mortality, and landscape structure. This project studies distribution and coexistence at the urban–wildland edge — where the animals are, how they move, and where their movement meets the roads.

title: Wild Cats at the Urban Edge
section: Ten counties, roughly eight million people
text:
Ten counties, roughly eight million people
The study area is the ten-county San Francisco Bay Area: Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Santa Cruz, Solano, and Sonoma. Roughly eight million people live inside this frame, next to a patchwork of parks, watershed lands, ranch easements, and open-space preserves.
Pumas and bobcats persist here at the urban edge. The relevant questions are about movement, permeability, and coexistence.

title: Wild Cats at the Urban Edge
text:
Two species, two analysis
The two species are analysed in parallel and never aggregated.









Puma
Bobcat




Occurrence records
Sparse
Abundant


Location sensitivity
High — coarsened on publish
Low


Home range
Very large (100s of km²)
Small (10s of km²)


Primary story
Isolation and connectivity
Occupancy and distribution


Primary method
Least-cost paths and corridors
Occupancy models, KDE, Gi*



The puma data has 1,028 precise, publicly shared occurrence points inside the study frame. That number is small for an animal that ranges over hundreds of square kilometres, so the puma work is built around connectivity: where the core habitat patches are, and how an animal could move between them. The precise points are never published — every puma map is generalised first.
The bobcat track is the opposite. Records are abundant, so the work is about distribution: which open-space units bobcats occupy, and which landscape characteristics best explain that pattern.

title: Wild Cats at the Urban Edge
text:
Five questions
The analysis is organised around five questions:

Landscape. How is protected open space distributed across the ten counties, and how connected or fragmented is it from the view of a wide-ranging carnivore?
Bobcat. Where are bobcats present across open-space units, and which landscape characteristics best explain that pattern?
Puma. Where are the likely movement corridors between core habitat patches, and where do those corridors cross major roads and high-traffic barriers?
Both. Where do the modeled puma corridors cross major roads and high-traffic barriers, and where is wildlife–vehicle collision risk therefore concentrated? Direct mortality records are pending; the road crossings serve as the interim risk proxy.
Cross-cutting. How much of the apparent spatial pattern reflects true distribution, and how much reflects observer and detection effort?

The fifth question is treated as a result. Detection effort shapes every descriptive layer in the project, and the two species answer it in opposite ways: the bobcat occupancy model corrects for effort, while the puma corridors do not depend on it.

title: Where Bobcats Are, and Why?
text: The bobcat (Lynx rufus) is a mid-sized wild cat, about twice the weight of a large house cat, with a short “bobbed” tail, tufted ears, and a spotted coat. It is the most common wild cat in North America and ranges across most of the continent. Bobcats are adaptable: they live in forest, chaparral, farmland, and the green edges of cities, and they hunt mostly rabbits and rodents. In the Bay Area they move through parks, watershed land, and suburban open space, which is why their records are plenty and their occupancy is the question to ask: How much of the apparent pattern is bobcats and how much is people with cameras and phones? The occupancy model is built to separate the two.

title: Where Bobcats Are, and Why?
text:
Occupancy
A raw map of bobcat sightings shows where people looked as much as where bobcats are. An occupancy model separates those two. It treats each open-space unit as a site visited repeatedly, models the chance of detecting a bobcat given that it is present, and from that estimates the chance the unit is occupied at all. The detection part absorbs the effort; the occupancy part is what’s left.
The fit is a single-species occupancy model over 845 open-space units, built in a fixed two-stage order: the detection sub-model first, then occupancy with the detection structure held fixed. The covariate sets and the selection rule were written down before any fitted number was looked at, so the result is a test of a pre-registered model, not a search for one that fit.

title: Where Bobcats Are, and Why?
text:
Detection is effort
The detection result is blunt. The single covariate is a per-visit record-count effort proxy, and it dominates: more recording effort, far higher detection. Against a no-effort null the effort model is better by an AICc gap of 408.
This is the whole reason the occupancy model exists. A sightings map would read that effort as bobcat distribution. The model reads it as effort and sets it aside, so the occupancy surface underneath is not just a map of where people were looking.

title: Where Bobcats Are, and Why?
text:
What explains occupancy
With effort handled, three landscape parameters shape where bobcats are. The pattern needs all three parts together — terrain, land cover, and human footprint. The model that keeps only one of them falls far behind: a human-footprint-only or a land-cover-only model is more than 40 AICc units below the full model, while the full model and its near-twin carry 85% of the weight between them.








Figure 1: Bobcat occupancy coefficients (logit scale, top model m_full), with 95% confidence intervals. Points right of the zero line raise the modelled chance a unit is occupied; points left lower it. Elevation is the strongest parameter (positive); human modification (gHM) is the clearest negative. Tree cover leans positive but its interval touches zero. Terrain aspect, slope, grass, and housing density do not separate from zero.





Elevation is the strongest parameter, and it is positive. Bobcat occupancy rises with mean unit elevation — the higher, less-developed units of the Coast Ranges and Diablo are the strongholds. Human modification is the clearest negative. As the gHM index rises, modelled occupancy falls: this is the coexistence limit showing up directly in the numbers. Tree cover leans positive but its interval just touches zero, so it reads as a lean, not a firm effect. Grass cover, slope, terrain aspect, and housing density do not separate from zero in this fit.
Housing density enters positive but unresolved, while gHM enters clearly negative. The two are correlated, and the project lets gHM carry the human-pressure axis. Overall, the human parameters in bobcat occupancy are real and negative.

The occupancy surface
The map below is the model-corrected result: predicted occupancy for each open-space unit, after detection effort has been modelled out. It is the layer to trust for distribution — not the raw sightings, and not the kernel density and hotspot that follow.








Figure 2: Predicted bobcat occupancy (ψ) by open-space unit, from the model-averaged occupancy fit. Darker green is higher predicted occupancy. Grey units are not modelled — they lack covariate coverage, so no prediction exists. The surface covers the 845 fitted units; the 284 grey units carry geometry only. Detection effort has been modelled out of this surface, which is what separates it from the raw record maps below.




This surface is where the effort correction pays off. A raw sightings map would put the darkest color wherever recording is densest — near trailheads, near cities. The occupancy model moves the results to where the landscape supports bobcats: up in elevation, away from human modification. Where the two disagree is the effort bias made visible, and it is the heart of Question 5.

title: Where Bobcats Are, and Why?
text:
Kernel Density and Hot Spots
The occupancy surface is the model-corrected view. Two descriptive layers sit alongside it, and both carry the effort problem the occupancy model was built to mitigate.
Kernel density. A smoothed surface of where bobcat records fall. The smoothing scale — the bandwidth — is set by a pre-registered rule, because the default bandwidth collapses toward a tiny bandwidth that just maps the densest clusters of effort. Even with the rule, a kernel-density surface of opportunistic records maps detection effort as much as bobcat density. It is shown as a descriptive layer, not as an abundance estimate.








Figure 3: Kernel-density surface of bobcat records (500 m, precise records only). Darker green is higher record density. The colour follows a square-root stretch, not a linear one: density is heavily right-skewed, so a linear scale would show only a few peak cells and wash out the rest — the stretch makes the pattern visible but visually lifts the low values, so read colour as relative pattern, not absolute density. Masked and out-of-study cells are transparent, not zero.




Hot spots. A Getis-Ord Gi* analysis flags units with significantly high or low record counts relative to their neighbours. A raw-count hot spot is partly an observer-effort hot spot. So each hot unit is cross-read against the effort surface and labelled — TRUSTED where the cluster is not explained by effort, EFFORT-FLAGGED where it is. The map shows the label, not just the count.
The result here is mostly an absence. After false-discovery-rate correction, only six units are significant hot spots out of more than eleven hundred, against 224 significant cold spots. Bobcat records barely cluster into strong hotspots at all once the correction is applied. And of the six hot units, the effort cross-read trusts only four — the other two coincide with recording-effort hotspots and are flagged as suspect.








Figure 4: Getis-Ord Gi* hot- and cold-spot units for bobcat records, FDR-corrected. Red units are significant hotspots, purple units significant cold spots, faint grey not significant. Solid red is a TRUSTED hotspot; hollow red is a hotspot that coincides with a recording-effort hotspot and is flagged as effort-SUSPECT. Only six units are hot (four trusted, two suspect) against 224 cold — the weakness of the clustering is itself the result, and every count behind it reflects recording effort as much as bobcat presence. Source: sfdep Gi* with the Q5 effort cross-read.

title: Where Bobcats Are, and Why?
text:
Summary
The bobcat occupancy model corrects for effort and, where it does, its picture diverges from the raw kernel density. The puma corridors in the next section do not depend on effort at all — they are built from landscape resistance, not from sightings — so they converge with the density surface for a different reason. Same region, two species, two entirely different relationships between what was recorded and what is there.

title: What was recorded, and what is there?
text: Every map on this site is built from records that people made. People do not look everywhere equally. They look near roads, near trails, near cities, and in the months of survey drives and community bio-blitzes. So a map of where the records are is partly a map of where the observers were. This is the effort problem: how much of the pattern is the animal, and how much is the observer?

title: What was recorded, and what is there?
text: Every map on this site is built from records that people made. People do not look everywhere equally. They look near roads, near trails, near cities, and in the months of survey drives and community bio-blitzes. So a map of where the records are is partly a map of where the observers were. This is the effort problem: how much of the pattern is the animal, and how much is the observer?

title: What was recorded, and what is there?
text:
Two species, two relationships
A descriptive surface — a kernel-density map of records, or a hot-spot map — carries the effort directly, because it is built from the raw records. The two analytical tracks then do different things with that.

Bobcat — the model pulls away from effort. The occupancy model has a separate detection sub-model. It estimates effort and presence as two things, then reports presence with the effort taken out. So the modelled result is expected to move away from the raw record density.
Puma — the model never sees effort at all. The corridor is built from the landscape: land cover, human modification, slope, and traffic. There is no record-density term anywhere in it. So if the corridor lands on the observed record density, that agreement was not put there by construction.

The result is a divergence for one species and a convergence for the other.

Bobcat: modeled occupancy DIVERGES from the record density
The bobcat occupancy surface and the raw kernel-density surface do not match. The correlation between the two is near zero (r = 0.075).
The raw density is effort-shaped — high where people surveyed. The occupancy model corrects for that, because its detection sub-model absorbs the survey effort and reports the presence. A high agreement here would have been a warning sign that the model had simply re-drawn the effort map.


Puma: modeled corridor CONVERGES with the record density
The puma corridor is the opposite case:

The corridor runs through above-median record density along its whole length. The least-cost path sits at the 77th percentile of the density surface (median across the route), and none of it falls below the median.
The Coyote Valley pinch is at the 83rd percentile — high record density.
Of the record hot-spots the corridor crosses, six of seven are effort-checked as trusted.

title: What was recorded, and what is there?
text:
Kernel Density and Hot spots
The surface below is the puma record density (kernel density). On top of it are the two-tier corridor swath and the core habitat patches. The corridor band sits on the warmer parts of the surface.








Figure 1: Puma record density (kernel-density surface, 1 km) with the two-tier movement corridor and core habitat patches. The density surface is smoothed with a wide (5 km) bandwidth. The corridor band runs through above-median density along its length, including at the Coyote Valley pinch. Density is a smoothed record surface and is effort-shaped.

title: What was recorded, and what is there?
text:
The record hot-spots
The density surface above is smooth. A hot-spot map is sharper: it marks the open-space units where puma records cluster more than their neighbours, tested for significance. But a record hot-spot has two possible causes — real puma presence, or a place people surveyed hard:

Trusted — the unit is a record hot-spot and not an effort hot-spot. Real concentration.
Suspect — the unit is a record hot-spot and also an effort hot-spot. It may just be where people looked.

The map below draws trusted units as solid fill and suspect units as hollow, dashed outlines. For the puma analysis, about half of all hot units are effort-suspect — far more than for bobcat.








Figure 2: Getis-Ord Gi* hot-spot units for puma records, FDR-corrected. Solid red is a TRUSTED hotspot; hollow dashed red is a hotspot that also coincides with a recording-effort hotspot, flagged effort-SUSPECT.






Of the puma hot units, the effort cross-read trusts fewer than half; the rest coincide with recording-effort hotspots and are flagged suspect. Any hot unit resting on fewer than three precise records is drawn without a hover label.






NoteSensitive-data note (puma)



Precise puma locations are withheld. iNaturalist does not obscure mountain lions in California, so this project does not share precise records that could expose real animals if published as points. The density surface on this page is published only at a 1 km grain, which cannot be reversed to a location. No puma points, den sites, or kill sites appear anywhere on this site.
